instruction: This is a new issue for our pétanque club. Here are all the articles. Lay them out across as many pages as they need, put the photos I've uploaded beside the stories they go with, and then design the cover: pick the best photo for it, lead with the best story and add our logo.
paste:
A WORD FROM THE PRESIDENT

The busiest summer we have had

When the committee put up the festoon lights along the terrain in May, a few members wondered aloud whether a pétanque club really needed fairy lights. By the end of June the Thursday twilight league had forty-two players, a waiting list, and a small but determined group who would not go home until the lights went off at ten. I think the question has been answered.

Thank you to everyone who raked, rolled, marked out, made tea and kept score this season. See you on the gravel.

Paulette Marchetti, President

SUMMER EVENINGS UNDER THE LIGHTS

How the Thursday twilight league took over the club

The twilight league began as an experiment: six teams, one evening a week, no trophies and no rankings, just a game after work while the light held. It turned into the heart of the club's summer.

Why it worked

The format is simple. Teams of three are drawn from a hat at half past six, so nobody plays with the same partners two weeks running, and the last end starts no later than half past nine. Newer members found themselves playing alongside people who have been at the club for thirty years, and the thirty-year members found themselves, for once, being asked for advice rather than offering it unprompted.

What comes next

The league finishes for the year on the last Thursday of September, with a shared supper on the clubhouse lawn. The committee has agreed to run it again next summer, starting a fortnight earlier, and the lights will stay up all winter, whatever the neighbours say.

EIGHTY-FOUR AND STILL POINTING

Joan Whitlock has played at the club since it opened, and has no intention of stopping

Joan throws underarm, from a crouch, with a small flick of the wrist that sends the boule up in a high, slow arc and drops it within a hand's width of the jack more often than seems fair. She learned the game on holiday in the south of France in 1971 and has played, she reckons, three times a week ever since.

"People ask me what the secret is," she says. "The secret is that I've been doing it for fifty years. That, and I don't rush."

She still plays in the Saturday doubles, still refuses a chair between ends, and still keeps her own score in a small notebook that she has been known to produce, politely, when the official scorecard and her memory disagree. Her notebook has never yet been wrong.

POINTING OR SHOOTING?

A beginner's guide to the two throws that decide every game

Every throw in pétanque is one of two things. You either point, rolling or lobbing your boule to finish as close to the jack as you can, or you shoot, throwing it to knock an opponent's boule out of the way. Most games are won by the team that knows which to choose.

The grip

Hold the boule in your palm with your fingers curled over the top and your palm facing down. Let it leave your hand from the fingertips, not the palm, and you will find it spins backwards slightly, which helps it stop where it lands instead of running on.

Reading the ground

Before you throw, walk to the jack and look at the terrain. Loose gravel slows a boule down; a hard, bare patch lets it run. Pick a landing spot, not a target, and aim to drop the boule there and let the ground do the rest.

When to shoot

If your opponent's boule is sitting right against the jack and you cannot get closer, shoot. If there is space to point into, point. When in doubt, ask Joan.

NEW PLAYERS' MORNINGS

Come and try it on a Sunday

Every Sunday from ten until noon, club members run a relaxed session for anyone who would like to learn. Boules are provided, no experience is needed, and you are welcome to come along just to watch. Most of this year's new members started at a Sunday morning, and several of them are now on the Thursday league waiting list.

CLUB NOTICES

- The annual general meeting will be held in the clubhouse on the second Saturday of October at eleven o'clock.
- Subscriptions for next year are due by the end of November and remain unchanged.
- The terrain will be raked and re-levelled on the first weekend of November; volunteers with rakes are very welcome.
- Lost property this season includes two jacks, a sun hat and a single glove; ask at the bar.
